posts.post_content:
Short answer: Online Quran classes for sisters and ladies mean everyone involved in your lesson is female, your teacher, and usually the person who arranges your schedule too, so there's no mixed-gender presence at any point, on camera or off. If you searched for a "female Quran tutor at home," what actually solves that need for most women isn't a local in-home visitor, it's an online tutor you meet from your own home on your own schedule, which turns out to be easier to find and far more flexible than a local search usually is. And no, "free" sisters' classes online are almost always a single trial lesson or a recorded series, not an ongoing one-to-one class.

A lot of the searching around this topic comes from a real, specific discomfort, not wanting a male teacher, not wanting to be visible on camera to a man, wanting to ask a question about something personal without hesitation. That's a completely reasonable thing to want, and it shapes what an actual class looks like more than most course pages explain. Here's what genuinely changes in a sisters-only class, and what "free" and "at home" actually mean once you look past the search term.

What an All-Sisters Class Actually Means

It means every person present in the session is female: your teacher, and typically the coordinator who arranges scheduling and answers your questions before you ever start. It's not a mixed class where a woman happens to be teaching that day, it's structured that way from booking through every lesson.

For choosing a specific female teacher, credentials and teaching style matter as much as gender. This guide is about the class experience itself, what's actually taught, how comfort and privacy work in practice, and what's realistically free.

"Female Quran Tutor at Home": What That Search Usually Means in Practice

Plenty of people searching this actually mean a local, in-person tutor who visits their home. Finding one who's genuinely qualified, female, and available at a workable time is hard in most towns, and it usually means a narrow, unreviewed local pool with no real way to compare options.

What ends up working for most families instead is the same feeling of learning from home, on a video call, with a female tutor, without needing anyone local to exist at all. It's not a compromise so much as a wider pool of qualified female tutors to actually choose from, since location stops being the limiting factor.

What's Actually Covered in a Sisters' Class

The academic content mirrors any other Quran class, Noorani Qaida for beginners, Tajweed, Hifz, Tafseer, Quranic Arabic, and now the full Alim & Aalimah scholar course with a female tutor throughout, there's no separate "women's curriculum" for reading or reciting the Quran. What changes is the space around it: students can ask questions about topics they'd rather not raise in a mixed setting, like specific rulings around purification (Taharah) that affect prayer and recitation, without hesitation, since the teacher understands the context directly.

Some academies also offer broader "Islamic courses for ladies" alongside Quran classes, covering daily Duas, basic Fiqh, and practical questions about worship. In a genuinely sisters-only setup, there's no male presence at any point in the session, not the teacher, not an assistant, not anyone reviewing the class later. The other real difference is simpler than it sounds: not having to think about how you're dressed or seated for a class, or hold back a question because a man might be present, removes a layer of hesitation that otherwise slows a lot of women down in mixed learning environments.

What's Actually Free (and What Isn't)

  • Ongoing free one-to-one classes. Rare, and where they exist, usually limited-capacity programs run by mosques or community organizations with long waitlists, not a standing option most people can rely on.

If what you actually need is someone correcting your Tajweed or Hifz week after week, that's realistically a paid, ongoing class, the free options are a genuine starting point, not a long-term substitute.

  • What is the teacher's actual certification, an Ijazah specifically, not just general teaching experience?

Are online Quran classes for sisters completely private, with no male teacher or staff involved?

In a genuinely sisters-only setup, yes, the teacher and typically the scheduling coordinator are both female, and no male is present in the session at any point.

posts.post_title: Online Quran Tafseer Classes: What You Actually Learn (And How to Choose One)
posts.post_content:
Short answer: Online Tafseer classes teach you what the Quran's verses actually mean, not just what the Arabic words translate to, drawing on classical scholarly explanations like Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Jalalayn rather than one teacher's personal opinion. You don't need to know Arabic first; most students start with translation and build from there. And most "free" Tafseer content online is a recorded lecture you watch, not a class where you can actually ask a question, which matters if what you're really after is understanding, not just information. QuranlyHub also teaches Tafseer in Urdu as well as English, if that's the language you'd rather learn in.

A lot of people search for Tafseer classes without a clear sense of what they're actually signing up for. Understandable, most course pages describe it in fairly vague terms: "understand the wisdom of the Quran," "connect with the divine message." True, but not exactly useful if you're trying to decide whether this is worth your time. Here's what Tafseer classes actually cover, honestly.

Tafseer vs. Translation: The Difference That Actually Matters

Translation converts the Arabic words of a verse into another language, as directly as possible. Tafseer (Arabic for "explanation") goes further: it covers why a verse was revealed, what the surrounding historical context was, how classical scholars understood specific words and phrasing, and how the verse connects to others.

A translation can tell you what a verse says. Tafseer tells you what it means, and often why a specific word was used instead of a similar one that would have changed the tone entirely. That distinction is the whole reason Tafseer classes exist separately from just reading a translated Quran.

Which Tafsir Do Online Classes Actually Draw From?

This is the part most course descriptions skip, and it's worth asking directly before enrolling anywhere. Reputable Tafseer teaching draws on established classical works, most commonly Tafsir Ibn Kathir, known for its depth and its heavy use of hadith and narrations from the companions, and Tafsir al-Jalalayn, prized for being concise and accessible, often the starting point for beginners before moving to more detailed commentary.

A teacher explaining verses from their own general impression, without reference to established Tafsir works, isn't teaching Tafseer in the traditional sense, it's personal commentary. It's worth asking any academy which sources their Tafseer classes are actually based on.

What an Online Tafseer Class Actually Looks Like

Classes typically work through a surah or a set of verses together. The teacher reads the verse, explains the context it was revealed in, walks through what classical Tafsir says about specific words or phrases, and connects it to related verses or to daily life, then opens it up for questions. It's a conversation, not a lecture you sit through.

That last part is the actual value of a live class over a recorded one: you can stop and ask why a specific word was used, or how a verse applies to something you're dealing with, and get a direct answer instead of moving on with the question unresolved.

Do You Need to Read Arabic First?

No, and this stops a lot of people from starting. Tafseer classes commonly begin with the translated meaning of a verse and build the explanation from there, so a student who reads Quran in Arabic and a student who relies on translation can generally join the same class. Reading Quran with correct Tajweed and understanding what it means are genuinely separate skills, and plenty of people who recite fluently have never studied Tafseer, while plenty of Tafseer students are still working on their Arabic reading.

Free Tafseer Classes: What's Realistic

Free Tafseer content is everywhere, mostly as recorded lectures or YouTube series, and it's genuinely useful for building a general understanding. What it can't do is answer your specific question about your specific verse in the moment, or notice that you've misunderstood something and correct it before it settles in as your default reading of that passage. If what you actually want is discussion, not just information, that's the gap a live class fills that free recorded content structurally can't.

How to Choose a Tafseer Class

A few honest questions to ask before enrolling anywhere: Which classical Tafsir sources does the teacher actually reference? Is it a live discussion or a one-way recorded session? Can you ask questions about the specific verse you're studying? And does the pace match where you actually are, someone new to Tafseer generally benefits from starting with shorter, well-known surahs rather than jumping into lengthy, complex passages.

Not sure which tafsir to actually start with? Our guide on choosing the best Quran tafseer for your level breaks down Ibn Kathir, Al-Jalalayn and the Urdu options.

Wondering if you need Arabic grammar before any of this makes sense? Our guide on whether an Arabic grammar course is necessary before Tafseer answers that directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Tafseer and Quran translation?

Translation converts the Arabic words into another language directly. Tafseer explains the fuller meaning, why a verse was revealed, its historical context, and how classical scholars understood it, going well beyond a word-for-word rendering.

Do I need to know Arabic to take a Tafseer class?

No. Most Tafseer classes start from the translated meaning of a verse and build the explanation from there, so students who read Quran only in translation can follow along just as well as those who read Arabic.

Which Tafsir is used in most online Tafseer classes?

Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Jalalayn are the two most commonly referenced. Ibn Kathir is deeper and draws heavily on hadith, while Jalalayn is more concise and is often used as a beginner-friendly starting point.

Are free Tafseer classes online actually worth it?

They're useful for building general understanding and are a reasonable place to start. Most are recorded lectures rather than live discussions, so they can't answer your specific question about a specific verse or catch a misunderstanding before it sticks.

How is Tafseer different from just reading a Quran commentary book?

A commentary book gives you one scholar's written explanation to read on your own. A live Tafseer class lets you ask questions, get clarification on something you didn't follow, and discuss how a verse connects to your own life, in real time.

What should a beginner start with in Tafseer?

Shorter, well-known surahs are the usual starting point, since they build familiarity with how Tafseer works, context, word choice, connection to other verses, before moving into longer or more complex passages.

Does QuranlyHub teach Tafseer in Urdu?

Yes. Teaching Tafseer in Urdu, alongside English, is one of QuranlyHub's specialities, since the academy is Pakistan-based. You can request Urdu when you book your free trial.

Studying Tafseer With an Actual Conversation, Not Just a Lecture

Understanding what you recite is a different journey than reciting it correctly, and it deserves the same kind of real, back-and-forth teaching. Our online Tafseer classes are one-on-one, grounded in established Tafsir sources, and built around your questions, not a fixed script. Book a free trial class and start with a surah that actually means something to you.

What topics does a Tafseer class actually cover week to week?

There's no fixed textbook worked through page by page. Most students pick a surah or theme with their tutor and stay with it until the discussion feels complete, covering the context of revelation, verse-by-verse meaning, and how themes connect across the Quran, before moving to the next surah or theme.

Is Tafseer taught differently for kids versus adults?

Yes. Tafseer suits older children and adults who can follow discussion-based lessons, since it relies on conversation and questions rather than repetition drills. Younger children usually focus on reading and memorization first, with Tafseer introduced once they can engage in that kind of discussion.

posts.post_title: Common Tajweed Mistakes English Speakers Make (And How to Fix Them)
posts.post_content:
Short answer: Almost every English-speaking student makes the same handful of mistakes, softening Qaf into Kaf, pronouncing Dhad from the tip of the tongue instead of the side, skipping the throat engagement in Ayn, and rushing Madd until it's too short to count. None of these fix themselves with more reading. They're physical habits, and physical habits need someone else to hear them and say "do it again, like this," not more solo practice repeating the same mistake with more confidence.

Most students who've been reading Quran for years still carry two or three mistakes nobody ever corrected. Not because they're careless, because the mistake sounded close enough, nobody was listening closely at the time, and it quietly became the default. This guide covers the specific mistakes English speakers make most, why they're hard to catch alone, and what actually fixes them.

The Letters That Trip Up Almost Every English Speaker

These aren't random errors. They follow a pattern, because English simply doesn't have these sounds, so the closest English sound gets substituted without the speaker noticing.

Qaf (ق) becoming Kaf (ك)

Qaf is pronounced from the back of the tongue against the soft palate, deeper in the throat than Kaf. English speakers, who have no equivalent sound, almost always soften it into a regular "k." The problem isn't just pronunciation, it can change the word. Reading قُلْ (Qul, "say") as كُلْ (Kul, "eat" or "all") is a different word with a different meaning, not just an accent.

Dhad (ض) from the wrong part of the tongue

Dhad is meant to come from the side of the tongue pressed against the upper molars, not the tip. Most English speakers default to pronouncing it like Daal (د) or a heavy "D" from the tip of the tongue instead, because that's the closest sound English has. It's one of the hardest letters to self-correct, since the difference is about which part of the tongue moves, something you genuinely can't check by listening to a recording of yourself.

Ayn (ع) pronounced too softly

Ayn is a throat letter, it needs actual muscle engagement mid-throat, not just an open mouth. English has nothing like it, so many students either drop it almost silently or replace it with a plain vowel sound. The letter effectively disappears from the word.

Kha (خ) and Ghain (غ) softened into H and G

Both are produced further back in the throat than their nearest English equivalents. Kha often gets pronounced like a soft English "H," and Ghain gets flattened into a hard "G," both understandable substitutions, both technically different letters.

Ra (ر) with inconsistent heaviness

Ra changes between a light and a heavy (rolled, throat-supported) pronunciation depending on its vowel and surrounding letters, and English speakers tend to apply one version everywhere out of habit, usually over-rolling it even where it should stay light.

It's Not Just Letters, Rule-Level Mistakes Are Just as Common

Even students who pronounce every letter correctly often apply the surrounding rules inconsistently.

  • Inconsistent Madd length. The elongation on a Madd letter has a specific count, and it drifts, especially when reading quickly. Too short and the rule is effectively skipped; too long and it becomes its own kind of error.
  • Ghunna dropped in Noon or Meem Mushaddad. The nasal sound that should hold for roughly two counts often gets clipped to almost nothing, particularly by students who learned the rule but never had someone check whether they're actually doing it.
  • Ikhfa applied as a full stop instead of a partial nasal blend. Ikhfa is a "conceal, don't fully merge" rule, and it's commonly over-corrected into sounding like Idgham (a full merge) or under-applied so it sounds like no rule was used at all.
  • Qalqalah forgotten at a stop. The slight bounce on letters like Qaf, Ta, Ba, Jeem, and Daal when stopping on them is easy to forget entirely when a student is focused on finishing the ayah rather than how they're stopping on it.
  • Stopping mid-phrase out of habit. Pausing for breath at a comfortable point rather than a correct one can genuinely change how a sentence reads, since Arabic sentence structure doesn't always match where an English speaker instinctively wants to pause.

Why You Usually Can't Catch These Yourself

Recording yourself and listening back helps with some things, pacing, obvious stumbles, whether you're rushing. It has a hard ceiling with articulation mistakes specifically, because you're listening with the same ear that's already used to your own version of the sound. If Dhad has sounded like Daal in your head for years, it will keep sounding correct on the recording too.

Articulation points are about where in the mouth or throat a sound is physically produced, and that's not something you can hear from the outside reliably, especially in your own voice. This is the actual reason a live Tajweed teacher matters more here than for almost any other part of Quran learning: they're not just teaching the rule, they're watching and listening for the specific physical habit and interrupting it before it repeats one more time.

Mistake, Sound, and Fix at a Glance

MistakeWhat It Sounds LikeWhy It HappensThe Fix
Qaf → Kafقُلْ sounds like كُلْEnglish has no back-of-throat Qaf soundPractice minimal pairs (Qaf/Kaf words) with a teacher listening for the throat position
Dhad → DaalHeavy "D" from the tongue tipSide-of-tongue placement doesn't exist in EnglishIsolated drilling on Dhad-only words, with direct feedback on tongue placement
Weak AynAlmost silent, or a plain vowelNo throat-muscle equivalent in EnglishSlow, exaggerated practice building the throat engagement before speeding back up
Inconsistent MaddElongation too short or too longRushing, or never having the count correctedCounting practice on Madd letters at a deliberately slow pace
Dropped GhunnaNoon/Meem Mushaddad with no nasal holdRule known in theory, never checked in practiceTargeted repetition with a teacher confirming the nasal sound actually holds
Missed QalqalahNo bounce on stopping lettersFocus on finishing the ayah, not the stop itselfPracticing stops in isolation, not mid-recitation

A Practical Way to Actually Fix These

Trying to fix everything at once usually fixes nothing. What works better:

  1. Get an honest baseline first. Recite a page for a qualified Tajweed teacher and ask them to point out every mistake, not just the big ones. Most students are surprised how many small habits they've never had flagged.
  2. Fix one or two letters or rules at a time. Trying to correct five habits simultaneously usually means none of them actually change. Pick the one causing the most meaning-changing errors first, Qaf and Dhad are usually the priority.
  3. Drill in isolation before applying it in recitation. Practicing a single letter or rule on its own, repeated slowly, builds the correct muscle habit faster than trying to fix it mid-ayah while also tracking everything else.
  4. Have someone confirm it, every time, for a while. A habit that took years to form doesn't disappear after being told once. It needs to be checked across several sessions until the correct version becomes automatic.
  5. Move to the next mistake. Once one is solid, add the next. This is slower than trying to fix everything at once, and it's also the version that actually sticks.

Common Misunderstandings About Fixing Tajweed Mistakes

  • "It's just an accent, it doesn't really matter." For some letters, true. For others, like Qaf/Kaf or Dhad/Daal, the mistake can change the actual word being recited, not just how it sounds.
  • "Watching YouTube tutorials will fix it." They're genuinely useful for understanding a rule conceptually. They can't tell you whether your own tongue placement is correct, since nobody's listening to you specifically.
  • "If I've read this way for years, it's probably fine by now." Years of repetition make a mistake more automatic, not more correct. The earlier it's caught, the less there is to undo.
  • "Recording myself is basically the same as a teacher." It catches pacing and obvious errors well. It doesn't catch articulation mistakes, because you're judging your own voice with the same ear that already accepts the mistake as normal.

These habits get harder to self-catch the further you progress, see our guide on advanced Tajweed for what changes once your basics are already solid.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the most common Tajweed mistake English speakers make?

Softening Qaf (ق) into Kaf (ك) is probably the single most common one, followed closely by pronouncing Dhad (ض) from the tip of the tongue instead of the side. Both come from English having no direct equivalent sound.

Does mispronouncing a letter like Qaf actually change the meaning?

Sometimes, yes. Qaf and Kaf, and Dhad and Daal, are different letters representing different sounds, and in some words the substitution produces an actual different word, not just an accented version of the same one.

Can I fix these mistakes by listening to Quran recordings alone?

Listening helps you learn what correct sounds like in general, but it doesn't tell you whether your own recitation matches it. Self-correction has a real ceiling with articulation-point mistakes specifically, since you're judging your own voice with an ear that's already used to the mistake.

How long does it take to fix a deeply ingrained pronunciation mistake?

It varies by student and by mistake, but a habit that's been repeated for years typically needs several weeks of focused, isolated drilling with regular correction before it becomes automatic, not a single lesson.

Is it normal to still make Tajweed mistakes after reading Quran for years?

Very normal, and more common than most people expect. A mistake that's never been directly corrected doesn't improve with more reading, it just becomes more automatic.

What's the fastest way to find out which mistakes I'm actually making?

Recite a page or two directly to a qualified Tajweed teacher and ask for a full, honest list, not just the obvious errors. Most students carry two or three habits nobody has ever pointed out.

Getting an Honest Read on Your Own Recitation

The mistakes in this guide are common precisely because they're hard to hear in your own voice. That's not a reason to worry about it, it's the reason a second, trained ear matters more here than almost anywhere else in Quran learning.

Every tutor at QuranlyHub is Ijazah-certified and corrects pronunciation live, in real time, across Quran Reading with Tajweed and Advanced Tajweed. Book a free trial class and find out, honestly, what your own recitation actually needs.

Why do English speakers struggle with certain Arabic letters in Tajweed?

English does not have direct equivalents for several Arabic letters, like the throat letters Ain and Ha, or the emphatic letters Dhad and Ta, so English speakers often substitute the closest English sound instead of producing the letter from its correct makhraj (articulation point). A tutor who can hear this happening live is what actually fixes it.

Can bad Tajweed habits be corrected after years of reciting incorrectly?

Yes, though it takes more deliberate practice than learning correctly from the start, since the incorrect pronunciation has become automatic. Online Tajweed classes with a tutor who specifically identifies which letters or rules are affected tend to correct these habits faster than general re-practice.

posts.post_title: What Is Ijazah in the Quran? The Certificate Behind 'Certified' Teachers
posts.post_content:
Short answer: An Ijazah is a formal authorization, given by a qualified teacher to a student, certifying that the student has recited the Quran (or a portion of it) correctly enough to teach it to others. What makes it different from a normal certificate is the Sanad, an unbroken, named chain of teachers behind it that traces back through history to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). "Ijazah-certified" isn't a marketing phrase, it means a specific, verifiable chain actually exists.

Most parents see "Ijazah-certified" on a tutor's profile and assume it's the same as any teaching qualification. It isn't, and understanding the difference is the fastest way to tell a genuinely qualified Quran teacher from someone who simply reads well.

What Ijazah Actually Means

Ijazah (الإجازة) literally means "permission" or "authorization." In Quranic sciences, it's granted after a student recites the full Quran, or a specific portion, directly to a teacher, who listens to every letter and corrects every mistake until the recitation meets a required standard. Once that standard is met, the teacher formally authorizes the student to transmit that same recitation to others, in their name.

It is not a course completion certificate. Nobody receives an Ijazah for attending classes or passing a written test. It's earned only by reciting, live, in front of someone already authorized to certify it.

The Sanad: What Actually Makes It Verifiable

The part that separates Ijazah from an ordinary certificate is the Sanad, the named chain of teachers behind it. A Sanad traces from the student, back through their teacher, that teacher's teacher, and so on, generation by generation, all the way back to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who received the Quran through the angel Jibreel.

This chain of transmission has been documented and preserved since the earliest centuries of Islam, roughly the year 100 AH. A real Ijazah names every link in that chain. That's what makes it checkable, in principle you could trace the exact line of teachers a recitation passed through to reach any specific certified reciter today.

Ijazah and Qira'at

Ijazah is often tied to a specific Qira'ah, one of the authenticated modes of Quranic recitation. Most online teaching uses the Hafs 'an 'Asim reading, the most widely recited worldwide, and an Ijazah in that Qira'ah certifies mastery of that specific transmitted reading, not "Quran recitation" as a generic category.

How Someone Actually Earns One

The process is straightforward to describe and genuinely difficult to complete:

  1. The student recites the required portion, sometimes the entire Quran, directly to a certified teacher, over an extended period, not in a single sitting.
  2. The teacher corrects every Tajweed error, every mispronunciation, and every hesitation as it happens.
  3. Once the recitation consistently meets the required standard across the full portion, the teacher formally grants the Ijazah, recording their own name in the chain.

This is exactly why the process can't be rushed or self-certified. Reciting well in one lesson proves nothing about consistency across an entire memorized portion, which is the actual bar an Ijazah certifies.

Why It Actually Matters When Choosing a Teacher

Plenty of people read Arabic fluently and recite the Quran reasonably well without ever holding an Ijazah. That's fine for personal recitation. It becomes a real problem when that same person is teaching a beginner, because pronunciation errors that were never corrected in their own recitation get passed on and repeated in their student's.

An Ijazah doesn't just prove someone can recite well, it proves someone else, already authorized, listened closely enough to certify it. That's the actual guarantee parents are looking for when they see "certified" on a tutor's profile, and it's worth asking a prospective academy to name the specific chain, not just the label. Our guide on choosing the right online Quran teacher covers the rest of what to check alongside this.

Common Misunderstandings

  • "Ijazah" isn't one fixed thing. It can cover a single Surah, the whole Quran, or a specific Qira'ah, the scope varies and matters.
  • It isn't awarded for attendance. Completing a course of lessons is not the same as being individually assessed and certified.
  • A degree in Islamic studies isn't automatically an Ijazah in recitation. They're different credentials, testing different things.
  • It can't be earned entirely alone. The defining feature is another certified person listening and verifying, which self-study and apps cannot provide.

A certified teacher also catches something self-study never will, see our guide on common Tajweed mistakes English speakers make for the specific habits that need a second, trained ear.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Ijazah mean in the context of the Quran?

It's a formal authorization from a qualified teacher, certifying that a student has recited a portion of the Quran, sometimes all of it, correctly enough to be authorized to teach it to others.

What is a Sanad, and why does it matter?

A Sanad is the named chain of teachers behind an Ijazah, tracing back generation by generation to the Prophet Muhammad. It's what makes an Ijazah verifiable rather than just a claim.

Can you get an Ijazah without a teacher?

No. An Ijazah is granted by a person, based on that person listening to your recitation directly and certifying it meets the standard. There's no self-certified or app-based equivalent.

Is an Ijazah the same as a degree in Islamic studies?

No. A degree covers academic study of Islamic subjects broadly. An Ijazah in recitation certifies one specific skill, accurate Quranic recitation according to a named Qira'ah, verified through direct assessment.

Does every good Quran teacher have an Ijazah?

Not necessarily, some experienced reciters never formally pursue one. But for a teacher correcting a beginner's pronunciation, an Ijazah is the clearest evidence that someone else already verified their own recitation is reliable to teach from.

How long does it take to earn an Ijazah?

It varies widely depending on the portion being certified and how much of the Quran a student already has memorized correctly. Certifying the full Quran with a documented Sanad typically takes years of consistent recitation and correction, not months.

What This Means for Choosing a Teacher

"Certified" should mean something specific: a real teacher, a real chain, and a real assessment, not just a phrase on a profile page. Ask any academy to name it plainly.

Every tutor at QuranlyHub is Ijazah-certified with a documented Sanad, across Noorani Qaida, Tajweed, and Hifz. See how Ijazah teaching actually works in a live recitation course for what a session looks like in practice. Book a free trial class and hear the difference a properly certified tutor actually makes.

Is an Ijazah the same as a diploma or degree?

No. An Ijazah is a personal certification of authorized transmission, given directly by a qualified teacher after verifying a student's recitation meets the required standard, not a diploma issued by an institution. It reflects a direct teacher-to-student chain, which is why the teacher's own Ijazah matters as much as the certificate itself.

Does every Quran teacher need an Ijazah to teach reading and Tajweed?

Not strictly, but it is the clearest way to verify a teacher's own recitation was checked and approved by a qualified teacher before them. Asking whether a prospective tutor holds an Ijazah, and in what (Tajweed recitation vs a specific Qiraat), is one of the most useful questions when comparing online Quran teachers.

posts.post_title: Quranic Arabic for Beginners: How Much You Actually Need to Learn
posts.post_content:
Short answer: You do not need fluent Arabic to understand the Quran, you need about 300-400 high-frequency words, since those cover roughly 80% of the entire text. Most people who give up on Quranic Arabic quit because they started with grammar textbooks meant for full fluency, when the actual goal, understanding what you recite, needs a much smaller, more targeted vocabulary first.

This is the gap between what people assume Quranic Arabic requires and what it actually requires to get real comprehension. Here's the realistic path, and where it fits alongside reading and Tajweed.

What "Quranic Arabic" Actually Means

Quranic Arabic is Classical Arabic, the form the Quran was revealed in, not the Modern Standard Arabic used in news broadcasts or the spoken dialects used day to day across the Arab world. This matters because a fluent speaker of Egyptian or Levantine Arabic still needs dedicated study to fully grasp Quranic vocabulary and grammar, and a non-Arabic speaker isn't actually starting from as far behind as it feels. Nobody is reading the Quran the way they'd read a newspaper.

This is also a separate skill from reading the Arabic script correctly. Reading with Tajweed is about pronunciation, getting the sounds right. Quranic Arabic is about meaning, understanding what those words say. A student can read fluently for years without understanding a word of what they're reciting, and plenty do.

The 80% Rule: Why Full Fluency Isn't the Actual Goal

The Quran repeats itself far more than people expect. A relatively small set of high-frequency words, pronouns, prepositions, common verbs, connecting words, accounts for around 80% of the entire text. Learning roughly 300-400 of these words gives a student a working grasp of most verses without touching a full grammar curriculum.

This is the single biggest misconception that stops people from starting: they assume Quranic Arabic means years of classical grammar before any payoff. It doesn't. High-frequency vocabulary comes first and pays off almost immediately, full grammar comes later and refines what's already understood.

Root Words Do More Work Than Memorizing Individual Words

Arabic vocabulary is built on root systems, most words trace back to a three-letter root that carries a core meaning, and related words share that root with a shifted meaning. Learning the root for "knowledge" ('-l-m), for example, unlocks recognition of 'alim (a knowledgeable person), ta'leem (teaching), and ma'loom (known), all at once. This is far more efficient than memorizing each word as an unrelated item, and it's the difference between vocabulary study that compounds and vocabulary study that doesn't.

The Realistic Order to Learn It In

  1. Read Arabic script correctly first. If letters and basic reading aren't solid yet, Noorani Qaida comes before any of this, meaning comes after reading, not instead of it.
  2. High-frequency vocabulary. The 300-400 words that cover most of the text. This is where comprehension actually starts showing up.
  3. Root word patterns. Learning to recognize the three-letter root system so new words become easier to guess rather than each one being memorized cold.
  4. Light grammar (Nahw and Sarf). Sentence structure and word-form rules, added once vocabulary already gives some traction, not before.
  5. Tafsir alongside reading. Once basic meaning is there, reading Tafsir commentary on specific verses builds the rest.

Most people who quit did the order backwards, opening a grammar textbook in week one, with no vocabulary yet to apply it to. Grammar rules mean very little without words to hang them on.

A Realistic Timeline

For an adult studying consistently, 4-6 hours a week, a working grasp of most verses through high-frequency vocabulary and root patterns typically takes 6-9 months. Reaching a level where Classical Arabic grammar is genuinely comfortable, closer to full comprehension without leaning on translation, is more realistically 12-18 months of sustained study.

These numbers move a lot with consistency. Someone doing 30 focused minutes daily will get there faster than someone doing three scattered hours once a week, the same pattern that shows up in Hifz and Tajweed both. Little and often beats occasional and long.

Do You Need a Teacher for This, or Can You Self-Study?

Vocabulary memorization and root-word patterns can genuinely be self-studied, flashcards and repetition work fine for that part. Grammar is where most self-taught students get stuck, Classical Arabic grammar has enough nuance that misreading a sentence structure produces a confidently wrong understanding of a verse, and there's no built-in way to catch that alone.

A teacher earns their place here differently than in Tajweed. It's less about correcting pronunciation and more about correcting comprehension, catching the moment a student has understood a verse incorrectly and explaining why, before that wrong reading becomes the default way they read that passage from then on.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting with a full Modern Standard Arabic course — useful for other things, but it's the wrong Arabic, and most of the effort doesn't transfer directly to Quranic vocabulary and structure.
  • Skipping vocabulary to go straight to grammar — grammar without vocabulary is a set of rules with nothing to practice them on.
  • Trying to memorize word lists with no root-word structure — it works, but far more slowly than learning the roots that connect them.
  • Waiting for "full fluency" before reading Tafsir — reading commentary alongside partial understanding accelerates the whole process, it doesn't need to wait until the end.

Understanding grammar and vocabulary is the language foundation; putting that understanding into context is what our guide on online Quran Tafseer classes actually covers.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much Arabic do I actually need to understand the Quran?

Around 300-400 high-frequency words cover roughly 80% of the Quran's text. That vocabulary, plus a basic grasp of the three-letter root system, gives most students working comprehension long before anything close to full fluency.

How long does it take to learn Quranic Arabic?

With 4-6 hours a week of consistent study, a working grasp through high-frequency vocabulary typically takes 6-9 months. Comfortable grammar and closer to full comprehension is more realistically 12-18 months.

Is Quranic Arabic the same as the Arabic people speak day to day?

No. Quranic Arabic is Classical Arabic, the form the Quran was revealed in. It differs from both Modern Standard Arabic and the spoken dialects used across Arab countries today, so native Arabic speakers still need dedicated study to fully grasp it.

Do I need to read Arabic fluently before starting Quranic Arabic?

Yes, reading the script correctly comes first. Noorani Qaida and basic reading fluency should be solid before shifting focus to meaning, otherwise there's no foundation to attach the vocabulary to.

Can I learn Quranic Arabic without a teacher?

Vocabulary and root-word study can largely be self-taught. Grammar is where most self-taught students misread sentence structure without realizing it, which is where a teacher's correction matters most.

What's the difference between learning Quranic Arabic and taking a Tafsir class?

Quranic Arabic teaches the language itself, vocabulary, roots, and grammar, so you can read the text directly. Tafsir is commentary explaining the meaning and context of specific verses. They work well together, but Quranic Arabic is the tool, Tafsir is the deeper explanation.

Starting With the Right Expectations

The realistic goal isn't fluent Classical Arabic in six months, it's understanding most of what you recite without relying on a translation every time. That's a genuinely achievable target, and it starts with 300-400 words, not a grammar textbook.

QuranlyHub runs one-to-one Quranic Arabic classes built around this exact order, vocabulary and roots first, grammar layered in once there's something to apply it to, with an Ijazah-certified tutor to catch misunderstandings before they stick. Book a free trial class and find out where you actually stand.

How is Quranic Arabic grammar different from regular Arabic grammar?

The grammar rules themselves are the same classical Arabic grammar system, but a Quranic Arabic course applies them specifically to Quranic sentence patterns and vocabulary, skipping conversational topics (shopping, travel, daily chat) that a general Arabic course would spend time on but rarely appear in the Quran.

Do I need to memorize Arabic grammar rules to understand Quranic Arabic?

You need to recognize grammar patterns, not necessarily recite rules from memory. Most students learn to spot how a verb's tense or a noun's role changes by pattern recognition built through guided practice with real Quran verses, rather than memorizing grammar tables in isolation.

posts.post_title: Quran Classes for Homeschoolers: How to Actually Fit It Into Your Week
posts.post_content:
Short answer: Quran should be scheduled as its own subject on the homeschool timetable, at a fixed time each day, not squeezed in "whenever there's a gap." Homeschool families who treat it like Math or Reading, same slot, same routine, are the ones who still have a working Quran habit a year later. Twenty focused minutes a day with a live tutor beats an hour of good intentions that keeps getting bumped.

Most homeschool parents don't struggle to find Quran resources, there are plenty. What actually breaks the habit is that Quran gets treated as optional flexible time, the first thing dropped on a busy day, while Math and English keep their fixed slots. This guide covers how to actually build it into a real homeschool week.

Why Quran Slips in a Homeschool Schedule Specifically

Homeschooling already means juggling multiple subjects, multiple kids, and no school bell to enforce a transition. Core academic subjects usually get protected time because report cards or curriculum tracking demand it. Quran often doesn't have that external pressure, so it quietly becomes the subject that moves to "later," and later becomes never.

The fix isn't more motivation. It's giving Quran the same non-negotiable slot as any other subject, and ideally a live tutor who expects the child at that time, since an appointment is harder to skip than a personal intention.

Treat It as a Subject, Not an Add-On

Homeschool curricula usually separate "academic" and "extracurricular." Quran gets filed under the second category by habit, and extracurriculars are the first thing cut when the week runs long.

Put it on the actual timetable, same time daily, ideally first thing in the morning before the day's energy gets spent elsewhere. A fixed 20-30 minute slot, five days a week, produces far more consistent progress than an hour crammed in whenever the schedule allows, and it's the single biggest factor separating families who stick with it from families who don't.

The Actual Learning Path

Skipping steps to "cover more" is the most common homeschool mistake here, the same one that shows up in classroom settings too.

  • Complete beginners start with Noorani Qaida, Arabic letters, sounds, and basic reading, before opening the Quran itself.
  • Once letters are solid, move into Quran reading with Tajweed, correct pronunciation applied to real pages, not just rule memorization.
  • From there, some families add Hifz alongside continued reading practice, using the same Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil revision structure that any serious memorization program runs on.

A homeschool schedule makes it tempting to move a child into Quran reading before the letters are actually secure, since there's no classmate pace to compare against. That shortcut costs more time later than it saves now.

Parent-Taught, Co-op, or a Live Tutor?

All three show up in homeschool circles, and they solve different problems.

ApproachWorks well whenWhere it struggles
Parent-taughtThe parent reads Quran confidently and has time dailySmall pronunciation errors go uncorrected in both parent and child
Local co-op classA group of homeschool families nearby, kids like peer learningFixed pace, less individual correction, depends on finding a group
One-to-one online tutorWanting real correction without needing a nearby groupRequires a consistent internet connection and a quiet slot

The common thread in whichever approach works long-term: someone is actually listening to the child recite and correcting mistakes in real time. Reading silently or following along with a recording doesn't catch a wrongly pronounced letter, and homeschool parents who don't read Arabic themselves can't catch it either. This is the same reason a trained tutor matters for any student, homeschooled or not.

Fitting It Around an Already Full Week

Homeschool weeks fill up fast between core subjects, field trips, and co-op days. A few things that actually help:

  • Morning over afternoon. Energy and focus are highest early, before other subjects have used up the child's attention.
  • Same days every week. A rotating schedule sounds flexible but is harder to protect than a fixed Monday-Friday slot.
  • Short and consistent beats long and occasional. Twenty minutes daily builds more real progress than ninety minutes once a week, both for reading and for Hifz revision specifically.
  • Separate siblings by level, not by convenience. A shared class sounds efficient but usually means one child is bored and the other is lost.

Common Mistakes Homeschool Families Make

Skipping Noorani Qaida to "save time" is the big one, it doesn't save time, it just moves the correction work later when it's harder to fix. Letting Quran float without a fixed slot is the second. And treating a memorization app as a substitute for a listener is the third, apps are fine for repetition between sessions, they cannot catch a mispronounced letter the way a person can.

A Sample Homeschool Week With Quran Built In

What this looks like in practice, for a family running two core academic blocks a day plus Quran:

TimeSlot
8:00-8:30amQuran (tutor session or supervised practice)
8:30-10:00amMath and language arts
10:00-10:15amBreak
10:15-12:00pmRemaining core subjects

Quran goes first, before the day has a chance to run long and push it out entirely. On days without a live tutor session, the same slot still holds for independent revision, so the routine itself never breaks, only the content of the slot changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I fit Quran into an already busy homeschool schedule?

Give it a fixed daily slot, ideally in the morning, treated the same as Math or Reading rather than as flexible time. Twenty to thirty minutes a day, five days a week, holds up far better than a longer session squeezed in irregularly.

Should Quran count as an academic subject in our homeschool record?

Most homeschool families do log it as a core subject alongside language arts, since it involves literacy, memorization, and language skills. Treating it that way on paper also helps protect its time slot in practice.

Can I teach my child Quran myself if I don't read Arabic well?

You can support the habit and sit in on lessons, but pronunciation correction needs someone who can hear mistakes accurately. If your own Tajweed isn't solid, a live tutor for the actual reading portion prevents both of you from reinforcing the same errors.

What age should a homeschooled child start Quran lessons?

Most children start Noorani Qaida around age five to six, once they can sit through a short, focused lesson. There's no strict cutoff either way, younger children just need shorter sessions.

Is one-to-one online tutoring better than a homeschool Quran co-op?

It depends on the child. Co-ops offer peer motivation but a fixed pace; one-to-one tutoring is slower to arrange socially but corrects each child's specific mistakes directly. Many families use both, a co-op for community and a tutor for individual correction.

Can siblings share one online Quran class to save time?

It's possible but usually slows both children down, since they're rarely at the exact same level. Separate short sessions, even back-to-back with the same tutor, tend to work better than one shared class.

Making It Stick

The families who keep Quran going for years aren't the ones with the most elaborate homeschool plan. They're the ones who gave it a real, protected slot and someone qualified listening on the other end.

Can online Quran classes count as part of a homeschool curriculum?

Many homeschooling families integrate online Quran classes as their Islamic studies component, scheduling live lessons during regular school hours rather than treating them as an after-school extra. Your tutor can also work with the family's existing weekly routine rather than a fixed academy timetable.

How many days a week should a homeschooled child take Quran classes?

There's no fixed number, but consistency matters more than frequency; 3-4 shorter weekly sessions integrated into the regular homeschool schedule tend to work better than infrequent, longer sessions, since retention (especially for Hifz) depends on regular practice.

posts.post_title: How to Memorize the Quran (Hifz): A Realistic Guide for Kids and Adults
posts.post_content:
Short answer: Quran memorization is not mainly a memory skill, it is a revision system. Anyone who has watched a Hafiz work knows the real secret isn't a special brain, it's that they review far more than they add. Most students who "try Hifz and give up" didn't fail at memorizing, they failed at revising, because nobody told them revision was supposed to take three times longer than learning new verses.

If you are searching for how to memorize the Quran properly, this guide covers what actually works: the traditional Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil system Huffaz have used for centuries, why forgetting happens and how to stop it, realistic schedules for kids and adults, and the mistakes that quietly derail most attempts.

What Hifz Actually Requires

Memorizing the words is the easy part, most people can lock in a page after enough repetition. What's hard is keeping thousands of previously memorized verses fresh while continuing to add new ones. That's the entire game.

A student who memorizes a page a day but never revises will have forgotten the first Juz by the time they reach the fifth. A student who memorizes half a page a day but revises properly will still have all of it a year later. Speed of new memorization is the least important variable here, even though it's the one everyone obsesses over.

Before starting Hifz, a student should already read Arabic fluently and correctly. If letters are still shaky, or if Tajweed hasn't been covered yet, that comes first. A verse memorized with the wrong pronunciation takes far longer to fix later than it would have taken to learn correctly the first time, and unlearning a wrong sound is genuinely harder than learning a new one. Our guide on where Tajweed beginners should actually start covers this sequencing in more detail, and Noorani Qaida comes before that for anyone still building letter recognition.

The Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil System

This is the actual method, used by Huffaz for centuries, and almost every serious Hifz program is built around it. Three Arabic terms, three jobs:

TermWhat it isHow often
SabaqToday's new memorizationDaily
SabqiThe last 1-2 weeks of memorization, still being locked inDaily, without looking
ManzilEverything memorized before that, the long-term bankCycled through completely at least every 2 weeks

The order matters more than people expect. A session should start with Sabqi while the mind is fresh, then Manzil, and only then new Sabaq at the end. Revision before new material, every time, not the other way around. Most self-taught students do it backwards, they memorize new verses first while they're motivated, then run out of energy for revision, and that's exactly how the backlog starts.

For a beginner, Sabaq is usually 3 to 5 lines a day, not more. It sounds slow, and it is slow, but a slower pace with intact revision beats a fast pace that quietly bleeds out old memorization every month.

Why Manzil Is the One People Skip, and Why That's the Mistake

Sabaq feels productive because there's visible progress. Manzil feels like nothing, you're just repeating things you already know. That feeling is exactly why it gets dropped first when time is tight, and it's exactly the wrong thing to drop. Older memorization doesn't fade evenly, it fades fastest in the portions you haven't touched recently, and once a Surah has genuinely slipped, re-fixing it takes longer than the original memorization did.

A rough rule that holds up in practice: for every hour spent on new memorization, plan on two to three hours of revision. That ratio feels wrong to most beginners until they've lived through losing a Juz they thought was solid.

Why Students Forget, and What Actually Fixes It

Forgetting isn't a sign that Hifz "isn't for you." It's what happens to any memorized material without spaced review, and the fix is mechanical, not motivational.

The Spaced Repetition Pattern That Works

New material needs to be touched at expanding intervals, not just once a week. A pattern that holds up well in practice: revise the new portion several times in the same session, again an hour later, once more before sleeping, then daily for the following week, then folded into the weekly Manzil cycle. Roughly: same day, +1 day, +3 days, +7 days, +30 days. Skip the early repetitions and the later ones get much harder.

Common Reasons Hifz Stalls

  • Adding new verses faster than revision can absorb them — the backlog grows quietly until a whole Juz needs re-learning.
  • Switching Mushaf editions mid-way — the brain memorizes page position and line breaks as much as the words themselves; changing the print layout resets part of that.
  • No one checking the recitation — small errors (a similar-sounding word swapped in, a stress mark missed) go uncorrected and become permanent without a listener.
  • Long gaps after a good start — a missed week early on costs more than a missed week later, because nothing is locked in yet.

That third point is the one self-study can't really solve. Reading silently to yourself, you cannot hear your own small mistakes the way a trained tutor listening in real time can. This is true of Hifz the same way it's true of Tajweed: the material can be self-studied, the correction cannot.

Realistic Schedules by Commitment Level

"How long does Hifz take" doesn't have one answer, it depends entirely on daily time and consistency, not talent.

Daily commitmentNew memorization paceRough full-Quran timeline
20-30 min/day, child, with a tutor3-5 lines5-7 years
45-60 min/day, older child or teenHalf a page3-4 years
1-2 hours/day, adult, consistent1 page2-3 years
Full-time, intensive program1-2 pages1-2 years

These are averages, not promises, students who fall behind on revision take longer regardless of pace, and students who protect their Manzil time can beat these numbers. The honest takeaway: a realistic slow pace that survives contact with real life beats an ambitious pace that collapses after two months.

Hifz for Kids vs Adults: What Actually Differs

Children

Kids generally have an easier time with raw memorization and a harder time with sustained discipline. Short, frequent sessions work better than long ones, and the Sabaq portion should stay genuinely small, 3-5 lines is normal, not a sign of slow progress. What breaks a child's Hifz journey is usually not ability, it's a parent or teacher pushing pace ahead of what daily revision can hold, which produces a child who "knows" a lot on paper but can't actually recite most of it reliably six months later.

Our guide on keeping kids motivated in Quran lessons covers the day-to-day side of this. For Hifz specifically, small visible wins (finishing a Surah, not just a page count) tend to matter more to a child's motivation than raw speed.

Adults

Adults usually have the opposite problem: better discipline, worse raw memorization speed, and a lot less spare time. The fix isn't to force a child's pace, it's to lean harder into the revision system, since consistency compensates for slower recall far better than motivation alone does. An adult who reliably does 30 minutes daily will out-memorize one who does two hours twice a week, even though the weekly total is similar. Consistency beats volume here, every time.

Adults starting Hifz later in life sometimes worry it's "too late." It isn't. The revision system works the same at any age, it just needs to be respected the same way.

Alone, With an App, or With a Tutor?

All three can memorize the words. The difference is in what catches mistakes.

  • Alone: works for people with strong existing Tajweed and real self-discipline, but errors go uncaught for a long time.
  • Apps and recordings: useful for the repetition side of Sabaq and Sabqi, genuinely helpful as a supplement, but they can't listen to your specific recitation and correct it.
  • With a tutor: the only option that catches mistakes as they happen, structures the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil cycle properly, and keeps a student honest about revision instead of letting it slide when life gets busy.

Most successful Hifz journeys use a tutor for structure and correction, and apps or personal recitation for extra practice between sessions, not one or the other exclusively.

What to Do If You've Already Fallen Behind

This happens to most people at some point, a busy month, an illness, a change in schedule, and a chunk of Manzil goes quiet. The fix is not to panic-memorize new material to "make up for it," and it's not to abandon the attempt either.

Stop adding new Sabaq for a short period and run a dedicated Manzil recovery cycle: go back through everything, section by section, at a slower pace than usual, with a listener checking each portion. It takes less time than people fear, memory that's slipped but not gone comes back faster than learning it fresh did. Once the backlog is cleared, resume the normal cycle, ideally at a slightly slower Sabaq pace than before, since that pace was probably part of why the backlog built up.

Not sure yet whether to commit, or just want to see how a real trial class works first? Our guide to what a free online Hifz trial class actually covers lays out exactly what to expect before you enrol.

Ready to see real numbers? Our guide on how the Hifz program works, what it costs, and how to enroll covers the practical side.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to memorize the whole Quran?

It depends on daily time and consistency far more than ability. A child doing 20-30 minutes daily with a tutor typically takes 5-7 years; a consistent adult doing an hour or two a day can finish in 2-3 years. Full-time intensive programs can do it in 1-2 years. These are averages, not guarantees.

What is the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil system?

It's the traditional three-part Hifz structure: Sabaq is today's new memorization, Sabqi is the last one to two weeks of material still being locked in, and Manzil is everything memorized before that, cycled through completely at least every two weeks. Sessions should cover Sabqi and Manzil before adding new Sabaq.

Why do I keep forgetting what I've memorized?

Almost always because revision isn't keeping pace with new memorization. A rough working ratio is two to three hours of revision for every hour of new material. Spaced repetition, touching new verses same-day, next-day, then at expanding intervals, prevents most of this before it starts.

Should I learn Tajweed before starting Hifz?

Yes, ideally. A verse memorized with incorrect pronunciation takes longer to fix later than it would have taken to learn correctly from the start, and the wrong sound becomes just as memorized as the right words.

Can adults start Hifz, or is it too late?

There's no age limit. Adults typically memorize more slowly than children but have better discipline, and the same revision system works at any age. Consistency matters far more than starting age.

Is it better to memorize alone or with a tutor?

A tutor is the only option that can catch small recitation mistakes in real time and keep the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil cycle properly structured. Self-study and memorization apps are useful as supplements for extra repetition, not as replacements for a listener.

What should I do if I've forgotten a large portion I already memorized?

Pause new memorization and run a focused Manzil recovery cycle: go back through the forgotten sections with a listener, at a slower pace than normal, until they're solid again. It's usually faster than the original memorization was. Resume new Sabaq afterward, ideally at a slightly slower pace than before.

Starting Hifz Properly

The students who finish aren't the ones who memorized fastest in month one. They're the ones who protected their revision time even when it felt slow and unglamorous. Get the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil balance right from day one, and the rest is just time.

QuranlyHub runs structured one-to-one Hifz classes for kids and adults, built around daily new-lesson-plus-revision cycles with an Ijazah-certified tutor listening to every recitation. If reading fluency isn't there yet, we start with Tajweed first. Book a free trial class and get an honest assessment of where to actually start.

What is the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil system mentioned in Hifz guides?

It is the three-part revision structure traditional Hifz programs use: sabaq is the new portion memorized that day, sabqi is recent memorization still being solidified through repetition, and manzil is older, already-memorized portions revised on rotation so nothing is quietly forgotten months later.

Can I memorize Quran online without a teacher checking my recitation?

You can memorize text on your own, but without a teacher listening, small pronunciation and Tajweed errors get memorized right along with the words and become hard habits to unlearn later. Online Hifz classes keep the flexibility of self-paced memorization while adding a tutor who checks every sabaq, sabqi, and manzil session live.
